2026-11-11.q: Which statement best captures the main point of the passage?
opts: Unions have rejected a 7.75% pay offer and will strike on Thursday.
The Government has published the full terms of a new public sector pension scheme.
An overnight pay agreement worth 10.75% over 33 months has averted Thursday's public sector strike.
Fórsa and Siptu have agreed to cancel all demonstrations planned for the EU summits.
2026-11-11.exp: The passage opens by saying the strike "has been averted following protracted overnight negotiations that culminated in a pay agreement", and the deal "provides for a cumulative increase of 10.75%" over "a 33-month period". The 7.75% offer was rejected earlier (A), the full terms "have not yet been published" (B), and nothing says the unions made an agreement about the summits (D).

2026-11-11.q: What can be inferred about the remaining consultation with the ICTU public services committee?
opts: It is likely to reject the agreement and revive the strike.
It has already taken place and approved the deal.
It will decide how the €5 billion is divided between unions.
It is not expected to stand in the way of the strike being called off.
2026-11-11.exp: Negotiators must still "consult the remaining affiliates", but "the formal cancellation of the strike is anticipated to be a mere formality", so no obstacle is expected. The consultation has not yet happened (B), rejection is the opposite of what is expected (A), and dividing the money is never mentioned (C).

2026-11-11.q: Why does the writer mention that Dublin is hosting EU summits?
opts: To explain why the strike had been planned for Thursday.
To show why the agreement came at a particularly convenient time for the Government.
To suggest that EU leaders helped to negotiate the deal.
To argue that public servants should not have threatened to strike.
2026-11-11.exp: The final paragraph says "The timing is particularly advantageous for the Government, as Dublin is simultaneously hosting EU summits", so the detail shows why the deal was convenient. EU leaders are not said to have taken part (C), the writer does not criticise the unions (D), and the summits are not given as the reason for the strike date (A).

2026-11-11-2.q: Which statement best captures the main point of the passage?
opts: After a four-month dispute over a new flat fee, an agreement means defence solicitors will return to legal aid work, with higher payments for heavier workloads.
The High Court has abolished the legal aid flat fee and ordered a return to the old system.
The Minister for Justice has resigned after the High Court criticised his fee model.
Defence solicitors have refused a new offer and will continue their withdrawal of services.
2026-11-11-2.exp: Solicitors "are expected to resume legal aid work in full" after an agreement; "the flat fee is retained; nevertheless, remuneration is now contingent upon the volume and complexity of work". The court has postponed its final orders, not abolished the fee (B); there is no resignation (C); and the solicitors are returning, not refusing (D).

2026-11-11-2.q: What can be inferred about the fee structure that existed before July?
opts: Solicitors received the same amount regardless of how many times they appeared.
It paid solicitors more for domestic violence hearings than for other cases.
A solicitor's payment for a case grew with each additional court appearance.
It had already been ruled unlawful by the High Court.
2026-11-11-2.exp: Under the old structure solicitors "received €240 for an initial appearance and approximately €60 for each subsequent one", so the total rose with every extra appearance. A single payment per case describes the new flat fee (A); the enhanced fee for lengthy hearings is part of the new deal (B); and the court ruling concerned the new model (D).

2026-11-11-2.q: How does the Law Society president's reaction to the negotiations come across?
opts: Dismissive, because he believes the reform remains unfair.
Positive, describing the talks as constructive and the deal as fixing the main problems.
Uncertain, as he says the outcome depends on the High Court.
Angry, because the minister kept the flat fee.
2026-11-11-2.exp: Martin Lawlor "characterised the negotiations as constructive, maintaining that the agreement addressed the scheme's two most significant deficiencies", which is a positive reaction. He does not call the deal unfair (A), make it depend on the court (C), or express anger (D).

2026-11-11-3.q: Which statement best captures the main point of the passage?
opts: The Censorship of Publications Board has decided to ban a new list of books.
Edna O'Brien's first novel has been published for the first time in Ireland.
Researchers have been studying the banned books collection in the Department of Justice for decades.
About 12,000 books once banned by the State are to be moved to the National Archives and made available to the public.
2026-11-11-3.exp: The passage opens: "Approximately 12,000 books formerly prohibited by the Irish State are scheduled to become publicly accessible", and the collection "is due to be transferred to the National Archives". The board's last ban was in 2016 (A); O'Brien is only named as one affected author (B); and the collection was "inaccessible to researchers" (C).

2026-11-11-3.q: What can be inferred about the Censorship of Publications Board?
opts: It was still banning books more than eighty years after it was set up.
It only ever banned books written by Irish authors.
It stopped working when the internet became widespread in the 1990s.
It banned books only for their sexual content.
2026-11-11-3.exp: The board was "established in 1930" and "The board's final decision to ban a book was made in 2016", so it was still active over eighty years later. This rules out (C); the list includes foreign writers such as Hemingway and Updike (B); and censorship extended "to depictions of divorce, adultery and violent crime" (D).

2026-11-11-3.q: Why does the writer list authors such as F Scott Fitzgerald, Ernest Hemingway and Iris Murdoch?
opts: To recommend which banned books readers should look for first.
To argue that foreign books were banned more often than Irish ones.
To show that the bans affected internationally famous writers, not just obscure ones.
To explain why the collection was kept on St Stephen's Green.
2026-11-11-3.exp: The writer says the list "encompasses internationally renowned figures such as F Scott Fitzgerald, Ernest Hemingway" and others, emphasising how well known the banned authors were. There is no reading recommendation (A), no comparison of numbers (B), and the authors have nothing to do with where the books were stored (D).

2026-11-11-4.q: Which statement best captures the main point of the passage?
opts: Ticketmaster has been fined by the EU for using dynamic pricing.
The European Commission is set to propose a Digital Fairness Act to strengthen online consumer protection in areas such as ticketing, subscriptions and deceptive design.
The European Parliament has already passed a law banning infinite scroll and autoplay.
Michael McGrath has proposed banning video game loot boxes across the EU.
2026-11-11-4.exp: The Commission "is expected to present the Digital Fairness Act", a proposal "intended to address persistent shortcomings in online consumer protection", covering ticketing, subscriptions and "deceptive interface design". No fine is mentioned (A); the proposal still needs negotiation with Parliament (C); and games would only have to "disclose the probability" of loot box rewards, not ban them (D).

2026-11-11-4.q: What can be inferred about ticket prices under the draft rules?
opts: Prices could still change during a sale, provided buyers are told the current and maximum price.
Platforms would have to charge the same price for every ticket.
Dynamic pricing would be banned completely.
Tickets bought in virtual queues would become cheaper.
2026-11-11-4.exp: Buyers would be "informed of both the current price and the maximum price applicable", and the proposal "is confined to disclosure obligations and does not regulate dynamic pricing comprehensively", so prices may still vary. This contradicts (B) and (C), and nothing says queue tickets would be cheaper (D).

2026-11-11-4.q: Which best describes the writer's attitude towards the final form of the law?
opts: Confident that it will be adopted exactly as drafted.
Hostile, presenting it as harmful to businesses.
Indifferent, giving no view on what happens next.
Cautious, noting that its final shape could still change significantly.
2026-11-11-4.exp: The last sentence says "The eventual outcome remains contingent upon negotiations with the European Parliament and the Council of the EU, which may introduce significant amendments", a cautious view. This is not confident (A), the writer does not attack the law (B), and does comment on what comes next (C).
